ev.a_bad_cough.text.3: The autumn damp crept into your chest and stayed until the festivals. You coughed so hard that the neighbor's dog barked back at you through the wall.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.4: A fever knocked you flat: for three days you shivered under every blanket you owned, then kicked them all onto the floor. On the fourth you felt hungry – a sure sign you'd pull through.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.5: The cold came at the worst time, right in the busiest season. You worked with a blocked nose and a croaking voice, and everyone gave you a wide berth.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.6: Your throat swelled until even water hurt to swallow. The old woman from the next street told you to gargle with a salty brew – truly vile, but a week later it eased.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.7: You got soaked to the skin in a cold downpour and by evening you were burning up. The night passed in delirium, full of endless stairs and strangers' voices.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.8: A dry cough kept you awake for weeks. You tried every remedy the neighbors offered – hot stones on the chest, mashed onion – and in the end it left on its own, as if it had simply grown bored.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.9: The sickness going around the district caught up with you after all. You lay flat for days, listening to the whole street coughing beyond the walls.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.10: Your head was splitting and every bone ached. You kept insisting it was nothing – until you fell asleep in the middle of a meal.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.11: After a long road in the wind you were chilled right through. For a week you went about wrapped up to the eyes and spoke in a whisper.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.12: A cough seized you in the coldest part of the year and only let go with the first warm days. You learned to sleep sitting up and to treasure every easy breath.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.13: The fever held for four days. A neighbor brought you hot broth and grumbled that grown-ups are worse patients than children – and you were too weak to argue.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.14: You were so hoarse that people at the market didn't recognize your voice. You had to explain yourself with gestures, and half the day folk laughed at you – kindly enough.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.15: It was a minor illness but a stubborn one: it retreated, then came back. You stayed in bed longer than you meant to and got up noticeably thinner.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.16: At night you shook with chills, and in the morning you couldn't get up. A healer woman set a bowl of pungent herbs by your bed and told you to breathe over it. It smelled awful, but breathing got easier.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.17: The cough dragged on so long that neighbors started recognizing you by it from afar. When it finally passed, someone even asked if you were all right – it had gone so oddly quiet.
ev.a_bad_cough.text.18: On a hot day you gulped icy well water – and by night your throat was on fire. For three days you couldn't say a word, and everyone agreed they were very peaceful days.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.1: {npc} sent word with travelers from a distant city: alive, well, asking for a warm cloak and telling you not to believe the rumors. Which rumors, the message doesn't say.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.1.E03: {npc} sent a letter from a distant city: alive, well, asking for a warm cloak and telling you not to believe the rumors. Which rumors, the letter doesn't say.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.1.egypt: {npc} sent a letter on papyrus. It opens as it should – "Before all else, I pray that you are in good health" – and ends with a request for cheese and a pair of sandals.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.2: Merchants passing through your district brought word: {npc} has settled into a new place, eats well and invites you to visit. All evening you went over every word in your head.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.3: A pilgrim on his way home tracked you down by name: {npc} wanted you to know {g=npc_sex:he|she} is alive and still remembers how the two of you stole honey from the neighbor as children. The pilgrim told the honey part with obvious relish.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.4: {npc} sent a little bundle with some travelers: dried berries, a skein of strong thread and, by word of mouth, a short 'I miss you.' You took a long time to untie it.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.5: A young stranger stopped by: '{npc} sends greetings.' It turns out {npc} is doing well now, respected out there and even a little full of {g=npc_sex:himself|herself}. You laughed till you cried.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.6: {npc} sent word through a trader you both know: survived the drought, mended {g=npc_sex:his|her} back, and wants to know if you've gone grey yet. You looked at your reflection in the water and decided not to answer.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.7: A neighbor came back from the fair and knocked on your door before even going home: {npc} is alive and well, trading at that fair, and says you're still the most stubborn person alive. So all is well.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.8: Wandering singers brought new songs and, as a bonus, a message: {npc} has recovered from a long illness and sends you {g=npc_sex:his|her} love. The songs were so-so; the message was better than any song.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.9: A porter you know brought you a gift – a handful of nuts from the place where {npc} lives now. The message: the nuts there are bigger and the people smaller. You'd know that sense of humor anywhere.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.10: The message took a long time to arrive, retold three times over, and some of it was clearly embellished. But the main part survived: {npc} is alive, well and thinking of you.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.11: A traveler asked for water and, after drinking, suddenly asked whether you were the one {npc} always talks about. He spent half the evening telling how {npc} praises you to everyone. You never suspected.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.12: {npc} sent an embroidered band with some travelers, along with a request: send seeds from home – 'where I live now, nothing grows right.' You gathered a whole little pouch.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.13: A traveling peddler laid out the news on your table like wares: roads washed out, prices up, and {npc} sends greetings and promises to come for the festival. You asked him to repeat that last part twice.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.14: The weary traveler who knocked late one evening turned out to be an old friend of the family. He said {npc} has built a house and sits on the doorstep every evening, looking toward your part of the world.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.15: {npc} sent word: alive, lots of work, little money, and the neighbors are a punishment from heaven. The usual – so nothing has changed, and that warms your heart.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.16: Word reached you through friends that {npc} remembered you at a festival and even raised a cup to your health. A small thing, but you walked around happy all day.
ev.a_letter_relative.text.17: A breathless little messenger girl rattled off what she'd memorized: '{npc} is alive and well, asks you not to worry, and wants the blue shawl back.' To be honest, you lost that shawl long ago.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.1: One stifling night you climbed onto the flat roof and watched the stars until dawn, wondering what your life would be like. The stars gave no answer, but your heart felt calmer.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.2: You couldn't sleep, so you slipped out past the edge of the village into the fields. The star-filled sky drifted slowly overhead and crickets chirped in the grass. You came back near dawn – happy, for some reason.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.3: You and a friend lay on the warm stones by the river until midnight, arguing about how many stars there are. You settled on 'a great many' and fell silent – it was better that way.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.4: In the middle of the night the silence woke you, and you went out into the yard. The sky was so deep it made your head spin. You stood barefoot on the cold ground for a long time, wondering who you'd become.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.5: While the grown-ups slept, you climbed the hill behind the village. From there you could see the lights of the houses and the stars – one set below, one above. You made a wish and never told anyone.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.6: An old herdsman showed you how to find your way by the stars. You traced the sky with your finger until dawn, repeating the names, and by morning you knew them all – or so it seemed.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.7: A shooting star streaked across the sky as you sat on the doorstep. You were so startled you forgot to make a wish, and spent half the night waiting for another. It came.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.8: The moon rose huge and orange, and going to bed was out of the question. You sat on the wall thinking that somewhere far away someone might be looking at the same moon and thinking of you.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.9: On a festival night everyone went off to the bonfires, but you stayed in the dark looking up. The noise of the celebration drifted from afar, the stars kept silent – and you were happy in their company.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.10: You bet your friends you could stay awake until dawn – and won. Toward morning the sky turned grey, then pink, and you realized that alone was worth staying up for.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.11: The heat wouldn't let you sleep, so you dragged your mat out into the yard. Lying on your back you counted the stars, lost count, started again – until you fell asleep smiling.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.12: A lone light crept slowly among the stars, and you spent till morning wondering what it was: a soul, an omen, or just someone's campfire on a distant mountain. You never decided, but it was a remarkable night.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.13: You'd quarrelled with the whole world, so you went down to the river at night. The water quietly carried the reflections of the stars away, and by dawn your grudge had somehow floated off with them.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.14: The old woman next door said every person is a star, only most don't know it. That night you spent a long time looking for yours and finally chose a faint but stubborn one.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.15: The night was clear and cold, your breath steaming. You wrapped up tighter and stayed until the stars began to go out one by one, as if someone were blowing out lamps.
ev.y_roof_stars.text.16: You climbed the old tree by the road and settled into a fork in the branches. Stars winked through the leaves, while below people passed by, never suspecting you were watching from above and inventing lives for them.
ev.f_holy_man.text.1: A strange man stands at the gate: barefoot, in rags, speaking in riddles, and looking at you as if he knows everything about you. The neighbours whisper that he is a saint – or just a madman. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.1.east_asian: A wandering monk in a tattered robe and straw hat stands at the gate. He speaks in riddles, laughs for no reason, and looks at you as if he knows everything about you. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.1.hindu: A sadhu stands at the gate – an ascetic smeared with ash, with a staff and a bowl. He says little but looks at you as if he knows everything about you. He asks for shelter for the night.
ev.f_holy_man.text.1.islamic: A dervish in a patched cloak with a begging bowl stands at the gate. He speaks in verse, laughs for no reason, and looks at you as if he knows everything about you. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.1.orthodox: A holy fool stands at the gate: barefoot in the cold, in chains, speaking in riddles and looking straight through you. The neighbours cross themselves. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.2: A blind old man with a pipe has sat down on your doorstep. He plays so that the neighbours stop working to listen, and between tunes he speaks of things he cannot possibly know. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.3: A man who has taken a vow of silence stands at the gate. He says nothing – only points at the sky, at your house and at his empty bowl. His eyes are as clear as a child's.
ev.f_holy_man.text.4: A hermit has come down from the hills – shaggy, gaunt, dressed in coarse sacking. They say he lived twenty years in a cave and is now going 'where he's been told to go.' Today, apparently, that means you: he asks for shelter.
ev.f_holy_man.text.5: All day at the market a strange man foretold rain, the harvest and someone's wedding – and half of it has already come true. By evening he knocked on your door, of all doors, and asked for food and a corner for the night.
ev.f_holy_man.text.6: A ragged old man with a bird on his shoulder stands at the gate. The bird studies you more closely than most people do, and the old man says it chooses where they spend the night. It seems to have chosen you.
ev.f_holy_man.text.7: This wanderer with a bag of herbs, they say, got some child back on its feet in the next village and took nothing for it. Now he's at your gate, thin and tired, asking only for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.8: In a downpour a barefoot wanderer stopped at your doorstep. He is soaked to the bone yet smiles as though the rain were a personal gift. 'Heaven sent me to you,' he says, and asks to come in for the night.
ev.f_holy_man.text.9: A man comes down the street chanting prayers mixed with words no one understands, a crowd of children trailing behind him. At your gate he suddenly stops, calls you by name though he has never seen you before, and asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.10: A grey-haired pilgrim has been walking to distant holy places for three years now. His feet are raw, yet he speaks as calmly as if the road were a joy. He asks for one night's rest.
ev.f_holy_man.text.11: A beggar sits by your gate – one, they say, that even the rich go to for advice. He said a single sentence to you, and you can't get it out of your head. Now he asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.12: At dusk a tall, thin man in a faded cloak appeared at the gate. The dog, which barks at everyone, lay down quietly at his feet. He says he has come from far away, will leave at dawn, and asks to be let in for the night.
ev.f_holy_man.text.13: The wanderer at the gate answers everything in riddles: ask his name and you hear about a river; ask where he's from and you hear about the wind. The neighbours tap their temples but keep a wary eye on him. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.f_holy_man.text.14: An old man, dried out like a twig, has been fasting – they say – for forty days. He eats almost nothing, but at your gate he asked for a sip of water and a roof for one night. His voice is surprisingly strong.
ev.f_holy_man.text.15: A wandering storyteller knows tales of holy men nobody here has ever heard of, and tells them so that listeners get goosebumps. He takes no money – he asks only for supper and a bed.
ev.f_holy_man.text.16: In the middle of the night there's a soft knock. On the threshold stands a stranger with a staff who says he saw your house in a dream and walked for many days to reach it. It sounds mad, but there's no madness in his eyes. He asks for a night's lodging.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.1: {npc} counted the savings in the jar and asked where half of them had gone. You had to confess to the new shoes – and then hear about the shoes until midnight.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.1.E03: {npc} counted the coins in the jar and asked where half of them had gone. You had to confess to the new sandals – and then hear about the sandals until midnight.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.2: {npc} found out you'd lent the neighbor the money set aside for hard times – without so much as a witness. The argument went on and on and ended with the two of you going to sleep back to back.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.3: At the fair you bought a beautiful and utterly useless thing. {npc} turned it over in {g=npc_sex:his|her} hands for a long while, then asked what it cost. The honest answer turned out to be a mistake.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.4: {npc} spent half the savings on festival gifts – generously, wholeheartedly and without asking you. You couldn't hold back, and the festival began with a quarrel.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.5: You argued all evening about whether to fix the roof now or wait till next year. The roof listened in silence and dripped in the corner. Nothing was decided, but plenty was said that shouldn't have been.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.6: The trader you owed money to showed up right at supper. When he left, {npc} asked, quietly and terribly: 'Why am I the last to hear about this?' You had no answer.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.7: {npc} thinks you're too generous with your friends; you think {g=npc_sex:he|she} is too tight-fisted. The quarrel flared up over a single flatbread and only burned out at midnight.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.8: You decided it was time to invest in the business and paid a deposit without discussing it with anyone. {npc} heard it from the neighbors. Of all the ways for the news to arrive, that was the worst.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.9: {npc} had been secretly putting a little aside 'just in case,' and you stumbled on the hiding place. You were both right and both hurt – the worst combination for a peaceful evening.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.10: Market prices went up again, and {npc} came home with a half-empty basket and a head full of reproaches. Somehow it all turned out to be your fault.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.11: You promised a friend some money, and {npc} is sure that friend will never pay back a thing. You argued until you were hoarse, and the worst part is that {g=npc_sex:he|she} is probably right.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.12: The quarrel began over a trifle – who forgot to shut the storeroom – and ended with a tally of every expense since the wedding. You didn't speak until morning.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.13: {npc} wants to save for the future; you want to live a little now. The old argument flared up again over a cold supper, and neither of you gave an inch.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.14: You let a traveling trader swindle you and paid three times the price. {npc} found out before you'd had time to come up with an explanation. The explanation didn't help anyway.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.15: {npc} counted the stores in the pantry and was silent for a long time. Then {g=npc_sex:he|she} started talking – and kept talking well into the night about who in this house can't count.
ev.a_money_quarrel.text.16: You invited guests and laid a table as if you were rich. The guests left happy, and until dawn {npc} itemized what all that merriment had cost.
ev.f_temple_build.text.1: The community is raising funds for a new temple: the old one is falling apart and can't hold everyone. The names of generous donors, they say, will be carved in stone by the entrance.
ev.f_temple_build.text.1.christian: The parish is raising funds for a new church: the old one is falling apart and can't hold everyone. The names of generous donors, they say, will be remembered at every service.
ev.f_temple_build.text.1.islamic: The quarter is raising funds for a new mosque: the old one is falling apart and can't hold everyone on Fridays. The names of generous donors, they say, will be carved by the entrance.
ev.f_temple_build.text.1.jewish: The community is raising funds for a new synagogue: the old one is falling apart and can't hold everyone. The names of generous donors, they say, will be written in a book of remembrance.
ev.f_temple_build.text.2: Heavy rains brought down the roof of the old sanctuary, and prayers are now said under the open sky. The elders have decided not to patch it but to build anew – bigger and sturdier. The generous, they say, will be long remembered.
ev.f_temple_build.text.3: Lightning struck the house of prayer, and only the sooty walls remain. The whole district is raising funds for a new one – some with money, some with labor. The donors' names, they promise, will be kept forever.
ev.f_temple_build.text.4: On great feast days people stand out in the street – the old house of worship has long been too small for the growing district. The elders are going from house to house, asking who will give what for a new one.
ev.f_temple_build.text.5: A wealthy neighbor has made a vow: if everyone together raises half, he'll pay the other half of the new house of worship himself. Now his people are going from door to door, and yours is next.
ev.f_temple_build.text.6: After an earth tremor a crack as thick as a finger ran down the wall of the old house of worship. People are afraid to go in, and the community has decided to build a new one before the old one crushes someone.
ev.f_temple_build.text.7: At the healing spring the whole district visits, people have decided to raise a proper shrine in place of the old shelter. Everyone gives what they can; the most generous, they say, will be remembered in prayers.
ev.f_temple_build.text.8: A revered teacher passing through your district remarked that the place of prayer here was too shabby for such a devout people. By morning everyone was collecting for a new one, and the neighbors are jealously watching who gives how much.
ev.f_temple_build.text.9: Good stone has been found on the hillside, and the community has decided it's time to build a new house of worship instead of propping up the old one with logs. Money is needed for stonemasons, and strong hands to haul the blocks.
ev.f_temple_build.text.10: It's been a good year, and the elders have decided to thank heaven with a new house of worship. After the harvest they're going from house to house asking each household what it's willing to give. The generous will be remembered, they promise.
ev.f_temple_build.text.11: The sickness passed your street by, and in gratitude people vowed to build a new house of worship. Now it's time to keep that vow: they're collecting both money and hands.
ev.f_temple_build.text.12: During prayers, rotten dust rained down from the old roof and everyone rushed outside. It was taken as a sign: build a new one, and build it now. The donors' names will be carved by the entrance, they promise.
ev.f_temple_build.text.13: The next village has built a new house of worship – carved pillars, painted walls – and your elders couldn't bear it. A collection has been announced: build your own, and better. The names of the generous, they say, will be displayed for all to see.
ev.f_temple_build.text.14: Your quarter has grown, and the nearest house of worship is clear across town. The neighbors have decided to build their own, right here, and are collecting from every household. Whoever gives the most will be remembered in every prayer, they promise.
ev.f_temple_build.text.15: An elder dreamed that a house of worship should stand on the empty lot by the road. The dream was retold all over the district, and now walls are being marked out on the lot and money collected from house to house.
ev.f_temple_build.text.16: The old house of worship has stood abandoned since it was sacked in troubled times. Now people have decided to bring it back to life – taller and finer than before. A collection is underway all over the district.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} beat you at knucklebones five times running. On the sixth you noticed {g=npc_sex:his|her} bones were suspiciously obedient.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.1.E03: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} beat you at knucklebones five times running. On the sixth you noticed {g=npc_sex:his|her} bones were suspiciously obedient.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.2: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} asked you a riddle you couldn't solve all day. The answer was so simple that {g=npc_sex:he|she} laughed till {g=npc_sex:he|she} got the hiccups.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.3: {npc} talked you into hide-and-seek and hid so well that you got genuinely scared. In the end only a giggle from the big basket gave {g=npc_sex:him|her} away.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.4: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} has learned to make string figures on {g=npc_sex:his|her} fingers and is now teaching you. You turned out to be a hopeless pupil, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} a strict and very pleased teacher.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.5: {npc} challenged you to a race to the old tree and won, of course. You pretended you were only acting out of breath – but you were out of breath for real.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.6: {npc} set up a game of market: pebbles for money, leaves for goods. You went completely broke, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} declared {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} the richest merchant in the world.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.7: {npc} spent the evening spinning tops with you, counting out loud whose spun longer. Somehow {g=npc_sex:his|hers} always spun longer – even when it fell first.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.8: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} made you play a game whose rules {g=npc_sex:he|she} invented as {g=npc_sex:he|she} went. You lost seven times in a row without ever understanding what you were playing.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.9: {npc} drew animals in the dirt with a stick, and you had to guess what they were. You got only the dog – and that, it turned out, was a cloud.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.10: {npc} begged you to play pebbles: toss one, grab the rest before it lands. Your fingers turned out slower than you thought, and {g=npc_sex:he|she} generously let you have another go. Twice.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.11: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} said {g=npc_sex:he|she} knew a game grown-ups always lose. It turned out to be 'who can stay quiet longest.' You lasted until the first funny face.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.12: {npc} built a fortress out of sticks and rags and declared war on you. You defended yourself bravely but fell under a hail of rag balls – to the victor's enormous delight.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.13: All evening {npc} played 'guess which hand' with you. You never got it right once: each time the hand held something that hadn't been there a moment ago.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.14: {npc} has learned a new counting rhyme and now starts every chore with it – who washes the bowls, who fetches water. Amazingly, the rhyme always lands on you.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.15: Your {g=npc_sex:son|daughter} {npc} started a word game and beat you with a word that doesn't exist. Arguing was useless: {g=npc_sex:he|she} immediately explained what it meant.
ev.c_knucklebones.text.16: {npc} raced bark boats down the stream with you, and yours got stuck on the very first stone every time. 'You're blowing on it wrong,' {g=npc_sex:he|she} explained like an expert.
ev.a_child_better.text.1: Today, for the first time, {npc} did the work better than you – and didn't even notice. All evening you grumbled, and all evening you were proud.
ev.a_child_better.text.2: {npc} did the haggling at the market in your place – and brought home more than you ever have. You acted as if that had been the plan all along, then secretly counted the takings again at home.
ev.a_child_better.text.3: {npc} fixed the thing you had fixed three times and finally given up on. Without a word, in half a day. You studied the work for a long time, looking for something to pick at – and found nothing.
ev.a_child_better.text.4: A neighbor came for advice, listened to you, then to {npc} – and did what {npc} said. You were offended right up until evening, when you realized the advice really was better.
ev.a_child_better.text.5: {npc} built a new hearth without your help, and the fire burns more evenly than in the old one you built. You grumbled that the smoke was going the wrong way – but it wasn't.
ev.a_child_better.text.6: Today {npc} spotted a mistake in your sums – politely, almost apologetically. You counted again: so it was. It stung for a minute; the pride lasted all day.
ev.a_child_better.text.7: A customer praised the work and asked who made it. You opened your mouth – and shut it again: {npc} had made it. You had to admit it out loud, and it turned out not to be hard at all.
ev.a_child_better.text.8: {npc} grew bigger vegetables on {g=npc_sex:his|her} little patch than you ever have. The neighbors came to look, and you pretended not to care while quietly asking what {g=npc_sex:he|she} watered them with.
ev.a_child_better.text.9: You'd been haggling with a crafty middleman for an hour and were ready to give up when {npc} stepped in. Two sentences – and the deal was twice as good. Where did {g=npc_sex:he|she} learn that?
ev.a_child_better.text.10: {npc} wove a basket – even, tight, without a single gap. Next to it your baskets looked as if they'd been woven in the dark. That evening you put it in the most visible spot in the house.
ev.a_child_better.text.11: Out of habit you started explaining how it should be done, and {npc} silently showed you how it could be done better. You snorted, tried it – and snorted again, very differently this time.
ev.a_child_better.text.12: Today {npc} finished {g=npc_sex:his|her} share of the work before you and came over to help with yours. The help was welcome, but it pricked your pride. In the end, pride in {g=npc_sex:him|her} won out.
ev.a_child_better.text.13: At the festival {npc} told a story so well that everyone held their breath – the very one you've been telling for years, which never sounded like that. You laughed loudest of all.
ev.a_child_better.text.14: {npc} settled a quarrel between two neighbors so wisely that both went away happy. You couldn't have done it – and everyone noticed, except {g=npc_sex:him|her}.
ev.a_child_better.text.15: You made stew your way and {npc} made it {g=npc_sex:his|hers}. The guests ate both, but asked for seconds only from {g=npc_sex:him|her}. You grumbled all evening, but still begged for the recipe.
ev.a_child_better.text.16: {npc} was the first to notice the weather turning and got everything under cover before the downpour. You, who had prided yourself on your weather sense all your life, got soaked to the skin – and were happy anyway.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.1: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} is at the door – puffy-faced, in someone else's cloak, reeking of drink. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asks for a little money, 'just until tomorrow.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.1.E03: Your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc} is at the door – puffy-faced, in someone else's cloak, reeking of wine. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asks for a little money, 'just until tomorrow.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.2: Someone's pounding on the door in the middle of the night: your {g=npc_sex:brother|sister} {npc}, swaying, asks to come in and borrow a little – 'to pay off a debt, or there'll be trouble.' {g=npc_sex:His|Her} eyes are cloudy, {g=npc_sex:his|her} voice a stranger's.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.2: You handed over the money. In the morning the neighbors told you where, and with whom, {npc} had been 'paying off the debt' until dawn.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.3: The festival ended long ago, but {npc} is still celebrating. Today {g=npc_sex:he|she} is on your doorstep – rumpled, holding someone else's cup – asking for money 'for one last day of fun.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.3: The last day of fun stretched into another week. You knew it would.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.4: {npc} has come to you without a month's wages: 'They were stolen, I swear.' {g=npc_sex:He|She} reeks of drink, and there are fresh scrapes on {g=npc_sex:his|her} hands. {g=npc_sex:He|She} asks for help before the master throws {g=npc_sex:him|her} out.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.4: You helped. A month later the wages were 'stolen' again.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.5: You've noticed for a while that {npc} drinks more and more. Today, for the first time, {g=npc_sex:he|she} came to you not to visit but for money – awkwardly, avoiding your eyes and breathing to one side.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.5: You gave it – and understood this wouldn't be the last time.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.6: {npc} stands at the door swearing to quit drinking – just as soon as the debts are paid. The debts need only a little, just a very little. The oaths come out slurred.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.6: The debts stayed, and the oaths were forgotten by the next morning.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.7: {npc} is sitting on your doorstep in the rain – soaked through, with a split lip and the smell of drink. 'Just a little for the road,' {g=npc_sex:he|she} mumbles.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.7: You gave money for the road. The road, by all accounts, ended at the first tavern.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.8: {npc} has fallen in with a merry crowd that hasn't been sober in weeks. Today {g=npc_sex:he|she} is at your door – red-eyed, cheerful at all the wrong moments – asking for money 'to settle up with friends.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.8: The friends got their share and started calling even more often. You heard their songs until midnight.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.9: After a bad year {npc} is drowning {g=npc_sex:his|her} sorrows. Today {g=npc_sex:he|she} came to you, sat on the doorstep and, without looking up, asked for money – 'just a little, to forget.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.9: You gave it. {g=npc_sex:He|She} did manage to forget – for one night.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.10: {npc} has brought the thing you once gave {g=npc_sex:him|her} as a gift and is offering to sell it back to you. {g=npc_sex:His|Her} hands shake, {g=npc_sex:his|her} eyes dart about, {g=npc_sex:he|she} reeks of drink.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.10: You paid for your own gift. The money was gone in a single evening.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.11: At dawn {npc} is standing at your gate: {g=npc_sex:he|she} spent the night who knows where and now needs money to settle with the innkeeper, who is threatening to call the watch.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.11: The innkeeper got paid. A week later {npc} owed him again.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.12: {npc} whispers at the door about a sure thing that will pay back double – all that's needed is a little up front. {g=npc_sex:He|She} talks fast and muddled, and smells as if the 'sure thing' has already been toasted.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.12: The sure thing turned out to be a jug of drink for the whole crowd. You never got double back – or half, for that matter.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.13: Late in the evening {npc} stumbled into your yard, knocked over the water tub and apologized at length. Then, sitting right on the ground, {g=npc_sex:he|she} asked for a little money – 'until better times.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.13: Better times never came. You knew it as you handed over the money.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.14: The neighbors are already gossiping: {npc} was staggering drunk around the market again. And today {g=npc_sex:he|she} is at your door, asking for money 'so as not to shame the family in front of the creditors.'
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.14: It didn't lessen the shame. The money went where all the rest had gone.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.15: {npc} stands at the door reminiscing about childhood – how the two of you shared your last crust. {g=npc_sex:He|She} goes on at length, tenderly, smelling of drink, and ends with a request: lend me a little, for old times' sake.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.15: You gave it – for old times' sake. The new times turned out worse.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.text.16: {npc} is on the doorstep, and for a moment you don't recognize the face: puffy, grey, with a stranger's smile. 'Just a little, until the end of the week,' {g=npc_sex:he|she} says, clutching the doorframe to stay upright.
ev.v_rel_sibling_drink.give.ok.16: The week ended, then another. You never saw the money again.
ev.y_first_job.text.1: The neighbors are looking for someone to do odd jobs for a little pay. There are two offers, and each one smells in its own way.
ev.y_first_job.text.1.E03: The neighbors are looking for someone to do odd jobs for a couple of coins a day. There are two offers, and each one smells in its own way.
ev.y_first_job.text.2: The potter at the end of the street needs a helper to knead clay, and a market woman wants a lively youngster to call out to customers. Neither pays much, but both pay.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.2: At the potter's – knead clay till your arms ache
ev.y_first_job.baker.2: To the market – call in the customers
ev.y_first_job.text.3: The tanner needs a helper to soak hides in the vats, and the smell there makes your eyes water. Meanwhile the shopkeeper across the way wants someone to deliver orders to people's homes.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.3: At the tanner's – soak the hides
ev.y_first_job.text.4: The rope-maker next door wants someone to twist fiber – dull work that leaves your hands blistered. And the dried-fish seller has an opening: stand at the stall and make sure nobody steals.
ev.y_first_job.baker.4: At the fish stall – mind the counter
ev.y_first_job.text.5: The dyer is looking for helpers again: by evening your arms would be blue to the elbows. And the baker wants someone to carry hot flatbreads around the streets before dawn. You have to decide by tomorrow.
ev.y_first_job.baker.5: At the baker's – deliver flatbreads before dawn
ev.y_first_job.text.6: The brickmaker promises pay for every hundred bricks you mould, and the woman who runs the eating-house will pay for washing bowls and running errands. The first will wear you out; the second will run you ragged.
ev.y_first_job.text.7: The weaver from the next yard wants someone to card wool and haul water for washing it – dusty, heavy work. And an old spice trader invites you to weigh out his goods and learn the prices.
ev.y_first_job.baker.7: At the trader's – weigh out goods
ev.y_first_job.text.8: The oil press needs hands – turning the millstone until your head spins. And at the market gate a middleman is looking for a sharp errand-runner. Both have already asked about you.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.8: At the oil press – turn the stone
ev.y_first_job.text.9: The carpenter needs a youngster to carry planks and sweep up shavings. And the neighbor who sells sweets wants help at her stall – rumor has it the helper gets a taste now and then.
ev.y_first_job.baker.9: At the sweet stall – mind the stand
ev.y_first_job.text.10: The fuller needs a helper to tread cloth in a tub of soapy water all day long. And the baker needs a delivery runner: before dawn, a basket of hot bread through the sleeping streets.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.10: At the fuller's – tread the cloth
ev.y_first_job.text.11: The building site nearby needs youngsters to carry water and small stones, paid every evening. And a cloth merchant is looking for someone to fold lengths of fabric and call in customers.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.11: To the building site – carry stones
ev.y_first_job.baker.11: At the cloth merchant's – call in customers
ev.y_first_job.text.12: The basket-maker by the river will take you on to cut and soak withies – your hands will be full of cuts. And at the crossroads a water seller wants someone to carry jugs to the shops.
ev.y_first_job.text.13: The dyer next door has broken his arm and needs someone to take his place at the vats. And at the market the greengrocer woman has lost her voice and needs a loud one. There's work to be had – take your pick.
ev.y_first_job.baker.13: To the market – shout for the greengrocer
ev.y_first_job.text.14: The felt-maker takes on youngsters – beating and rolling wool till you're drenched in sweat. And the bread seller wants a helper at the counter: hand it over, take payment, smile.
ev.y_first_job.fuller.14: At the felt-maker's – roll the wool
ev.y_first_job.text.15: The grown-ups say it's time you brought something home. There are two places: with the craftsman who grinds pigments – the dust there gets into your skin – and with the peddler who's always short of quick feet.
ev.y_first_job.text.16: Before the festival everyone needs extra hands: the craftsman next door wants someone to polish pots for the fair, the market woman wants help at her stall in the crush. The pay is festival-generous – but you don't want to miss the festival either.
ev.y_first_job.baker.16: Work the stall in the crush
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.1: One morning you noticed {npc} is no longer a child: a different voice, arguments about grain prices, and embarrassment when you ruffle {g=npc_sex:his|her} hair.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.1.athens: {npc} {g=npc_sex:cut off his boyhood curls and offered them to the gods, as Athenians do at the Apaturia festival|dedicated her childhood toys to Artemis – the way Athenian girls say goodbye to childhood}. You watched and couldn't understand where the years had gone.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.1.rome: {npc} {g=npc_sex:put on the white toga of a grown man for the first time and took off his childhood bulla|laid her dolls on the household altar – the way Roman girls say goodbye to childhood}. You watched and couldn't understand where the years had gone.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.2: {npc} brought home {g=npc_sex:his|her} own earnings for the first time and silently laid them on the table. You acted as if it were nothing special, then sat for a long time looking at that money.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.3: Today you suddenly noticed that {npc} is half a head taller than you. When did that happen? Only yesterday, it seems, {g=npc_sex:he|she} was running barefoot around the yard.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.4: In an argument with a neighbor, {npc} took your side – calmly, firmly, like a grown-up. The neighbor backed down, and you couldn't stop smiling all evening.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.5: {npc} asked you to knock before coming in. You were about to laugh, but saw in time how seriously it was meant.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.6: {npc} gave {g=npc_sex:his|her} old favorite toy to a neighbor's little one – without regret, even with a certain dignity. You watched the toy go for longer than {g=npc_sex:he|she} did.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.7: Over supper {npc} talked about business so sensibly that you forgot to correct {g=npc_sex:him|her}. Then you caught yourself – and realized there was nothing to correct.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.8: Today, for the first time, {npc} sat among the grown-ups at the festival instead of running around with the children. {g=npc_sex:He|She} carried {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} with dignity and a little comically, and your heart ached.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.9: You were about to scold {npc} for coming home late, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} calmly explained where {g=npc_sex:he|she} had been and why. The explanation was sensible. There was no one left to scold – a grown person stood before you.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.10: {npc} now gets up before you and has half the morning chores done while you're still washing your face. You grumbled that nobody asked – and wondered when all this had happened.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.11: You saw {npc} blush when walking past a certain neighbor's yard. You said nothing, only sighed: so childhood is over.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.12: {npc} asked for your advice – not like a child asking permission, but like an adult who values your opinion. It caught you off guard, and you answered better than usual.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.13: {npc} {g=npc_sex:has started speaking in a new voice – now deep, now cracking – and is embarrassed by it|has started doing her hair like a grown woman and is shy about it}. You watched and didn't recognize the child you once rocked in your arms.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.14: {npc} worked beside you all day as an equal and didn't complain once. In the evening you caught yourself talking to {g=npc_sex:him|her} as an equal.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.15: Out of old habit you reached to straighten {npc}'s collar, but {g=npc_sex:he|she} gently moved your hand away: 'I can do it myself.' It was said kindly, yet something inside you turned over.
ev.c_coming_of_age.text.16: Today, for the first time, {npc} stood at prayer among the grown-ups instead of at the back with the children. You looked at {g=npc_sex:his|her} serious face and couldn't understand where the years had gone.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.1: A learned physician who has treated your neighbors makes an offer: for a regular fee he'll look after the whole family – take pulses, advise on food and come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.1.ANE: A physician who has treated your neighbours makes an offer: for a regular fee he'll look after the whole family – give remedies, recite spells against illness and come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.1.E03: A Greek physician who has treated your neighbors makes an offer: for a regular fee he'll look after the whole family – take pulses, advise on food and come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.1.rome: A Greek physician who has treated your neighbors makes an offer: for a regular fee he'll look after the whole family – take pulses, advise on food and come at the first call. The old men grumble that their ancestors managed without Greeks – on cabbage and prayer.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.2: A well-known physician makes his rounds of the town with two pupils, taking on regular patients. He offers you the same: for a fee he'll call at your house once a month, keep an eye on everyone and come at the first summons.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.3: A young physician, just finished studying under a famous master, is looking for regular patients. He is earnest and polite, and offers to look after your whole household for a moderate fee.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.4: A visiting physician got a neighbor back on his feet when everyone had given him up for dead. Now that physician is at your door with an offer: for a regular fee he'll treat everyone in your household.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.5: A grey-haired physician with a box of remedies says he heals by ancient teachings and knows how to lengthen life. For a regular fee he's willing to call at your house and see that everyone stays well.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.6: The physician who attends the richest people in the district has unexpectedly offered his services to you too. The fee is no small thing, but he promises to take pulses, advise on diet and come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.7: At the market a man in clean clothes approached you, introduced himself as a physician and declared at first glance that your liver was not right. For a regular fee he offers to watch over the health of your whole household.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.8: A physician who trained in the capital has moved to your district. He's seeking regular patients among people of means and makes you an offer: he'll visit the house, take pulses and come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.9: An old acquaintance who became a physician offers, as a friend – though not for free – to take your household under his care: examine everyone monthly, give advice and come even at night if needed.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.10: Since last year's epidemic, people of means have taken to keeping their own physicians. One of them, tired and knowledgeable, offers you the same: a regular fee, and he'll be there when trouble knocks.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.11: A physician who is said to be strict but has never yet done harm offers to take your household into his care. He warns you straight away: you'll eat what he says and sleep when he says.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.12: A physician who knows hundreds of herbs and roots proposes a standing arrangement: for a fee he'll call on you, watch over the health of everyone in the house and keep the right remedies on hand.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.13: A physician from distant lands with a heavy accent heals, they say, differently from the local ones – and successfully. He offers you a standing arrangement: a fee every month, and he'll come at the first call.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.14: The neighbors all sing the praises of their physician: he takes pulses, gives remedies and comes at night. Today he dropped by himself and offered you the same – for a regular fee.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.15: The physician you once called to a sick worker stayed on and looked over the whole house. Before leaving he proposed: for a regular fee he'd look after everyone, rather than coming when it's already too late.
ev.c_h_family_doctor.text.16: The physician who has treated half the town names his price plainly: a fee every month, and your health becomes his concern. 'Curing the sick costs more than keeping the healthy well,' he says, and that's hard to argue with.
ev.y_bad_influence.text.1: An older youth from the next street, a dandy with a ring on his finger, invites you to the tavern tonight to play dice. 'Stick with me and you'll do fine.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.2: A crowd of older lads gathers behind the warehouses every evening to play dice for money. Tonight their ringleader – split eyebrow, wide grin – nodded at you: 'Sit down, beginners always get lucky.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.3: A cheerful young stranger with a fat purse and dice in his pocket has put up at the inn. He's looking for someone to play with and for some reason picked you: 'You look like a lad with a head on his shoulders.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.4: On festival night, when the grown-ups have other things on their minds, the older boys have set up a dice game right in the street by torchlight. They call you into the circle: 'Or are you still too little?'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.5: Your old playmate, whom you haven't seen in ages, now wears an expensive belt and throws money around. He says he won it all at dice, and invites you this evening to where they play for big stakes.
ev.y_bad_influence.text.6: In the evenings lads gather under the bridge by the river – throwing dice, arguing, sometimes fighting. One of them, quick and mocking, offered you a game: 'Bet whatever you won't miss.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.7: The trader's assistant from the next street whispered that there's a dice game in the back room of the eating-house every evening and that you'll get in if you come with him. 'Just keep it quiet at home.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.8: They say of one lad at the market that the dice obey him. Today he came up to you himself, tossed a die in his palm and invited you along tonight: 'I'll teach you how to win.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.9: You've heard the older boys bragging that one evening of dice can bring in more than a month of work. Tonight one of them invites you along: 'Don't be a coward, everybody starts somewhere.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.10: A young warrior back from a campaign is throwing his plunder around and inviting the lads to play dice with him. For some reason he's taken a liking to you: 'Come on, I'll show you how real men play.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.11: After work the apprentices gather in a corner of the yard and throw dice for their day's pay. The eldest held out the dice cup to you: 'Well – take a chance, or run off to bed?'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.12: When the market closes, a different trade starts among the empty stalls – dice by lamplight. A porter you know invites you along: 'The money that changes hands there – you wouldn't believe it.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.13: An older lad once helped you out in a fight and now reminds you: 'You owe me one.' The favor is simple – keep him company at dice tonight.
ev.y_bad_influence.text.14: You've met a cheerful fellow who always has money and never has work. Tonight he's inviting you to where they throw dice in the evenings: 'Stick with me and you'll do fine – guaranteed.'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.15: Your friends bet you wouldn't dare go where grown men play dice for money. The cheekiest of them is already leading the way, waving you on: 'Well? Or are you scared?'
ev.y_bad_influence.text.16: The travelers at the inn have been playing dice all night, and their shouts carry into the street. One of them, generous and a bit drunk, waves you over: 'Sit down, play a round – you've got a lucky hand.'
ev.c_h_wound.text.1: A trifling scratch from a dirty splinter has swollen and reddened in a week and throbs so hard you can't sleep. Your arm is hot right up to the elbow.
ev.c_h_wound.text.1.E03: A trifling scratch from a rusty nail has swollen and reddened in a week and throbs so hard you can't sleep. Your arm is hot right up to the elbow.
ev.c_h_wound.text.2: A fishhook sank into your palm; you pulled it out and forgot about it. A week later your hand is swollen, the skin around the wound tight and shiny, and at night your arm throbs so you can't sleep.
ev.c_h_wound.text.3: The neighbor's dog nipped your arm – not deep, you didn't even bother bandaging it. Now the bite is red, swollen and burning, and a red streak is creeping up your arm.
ev.c_h_wound.text.4: A thorny splinter went deep under your fingernail, and you couldn't get all of it out. The finger has swollen to twice its size, and the pain now shoots all the way to your shoulder.
ev.c_h_wound.text.5: At the river you cut your hand on sharp sedge – a trifle, the bleeding stopped at once. But a few days later the cut festered, your arm grew hot, and you've got the chills.
ev.c_h_wound.text.6: You grabbed a hot pot and burned your palm. The blister broke, dirt got in, and now your whole hand is red and the arm burns up to the elbow.
ev.c_h_wound.text.7: A broken pot left you a souvenir: a deep cut on your wrist. First it closed, then opened again – and now pus is oozing from it and your arm feels heavy and hot.
ev.c_h_wound.text.8: A frightened cat clawed your arm, and one scratch just won't heal. The skin around it has puffed up, and at night your arm throbs so badly you want to howl.
ev.c_h_wound.text.9: You skinned your knuckles on a stone wall while hauling loads. The scrapes crusted over, pus gathered underneath, and now your hand won't bend.
ev.c_h_wound.text.10: Gutting a fish, you pricked your finger on a sharp fin. Three days later the finger is dark at the nail, the palm is swollen and a red line is running up your arm.
ev.c_h_wound.text.11: Pushing through thornbushes, you scratched up your arms, and one scratch near the elbow has become inflamed. It's hot, hard and hurts with every movement.
ev.c_h_wound.text.12: A work blister burst; you paid it no mind – a mistake. Your palm is swollen and red, and in the middle an abscess the size of a fingernail has swelled up.
ev.c_h_wound.text.13: A rat bit you in the storeroom one night. The wound is tiny, but a few days later your arm has swollen to the elbow and you're swinging between fever and chills.
ev.c_h_wound.text.14: A tool slipped and gashed your forearm. You wrapped it in the first rag at hand and went back to work. Now the edges of the wound are puffy and weeping, and your arm is burning.
ev.c_h_wound.text.15: You scratched an insect bite on your arm until it bled. A trifle, you'd think, but it has swollen into a hard, hot lump, and the pain won't let you sleep.
ev.c_h_wound.text.16: You slipped and scraped your arm on the stones. You washed the graze half-heartedly, and within a week it turned into a hot, weeping wound that makes your fingers go numb.
ev.j_any_fire.text.1: A fire broke out in the quarter at night, and the flames have already reached the building where you work. Neighbours are shouting beyond the wall; somewhere children are crying.
ev.j_any_fire.text.1.rome: A fire broke out in the crowded quarter at night: the wooden upper floors of the tenements burn like straw. The flames have already reached the building where you work, and neighbours are shouting beyond the wall.
ev.j_any_fire.text.2: Someone in the next workshop knocked a lamp onto dry shavings, and within a minute fire was licking at the roof. Now the building where you work is burning too, and cries for help come from the windows opposite.
ev.j_any_fire.text.3: A dry wind carried sparks from someone's hearth across the whole quarter. The flames roar, roofs catch one after another, and the building where you work is already full of smoke. Somewhere nearby children are crying.
ev.j_any_fire.text.4: You woke to shouts and crackling: the storehouse next to where you work is ablaze, and the fire has already jumped the wall. Neighbors are running out in whatever they slept in; someone is leading the old folks out.
ev.j_any_fire.text.5: A dry thunderstorm without a drop of rain sent lightning into the roof next door. While everyone stared, the fire crept over to the building where you work. Beyond the wall someone is calling for help.
ev.j_any_fire.text.6: On a festival night an awning caught from the bonfires, then the whole row of houses – including the one where you work. The street is jammed with people, and children's cries ring out through the smoke.
ev.j_any_fire.text.7: The drying shed next door, packed with bundles of dry grass, caught fire, and the flames shot higher than the roofs. A minute later the building where you work was smoking too, and someone in the house opposite can't get out.
ev.j_any_fire.text.8: Before dawn you smelled smoke – and ran out just in time to see the flames engulf the building where you work. Neighbors are rushing about with buckets; somewhere a child is screaming.
ev.j_any_fire.text.9: At the eating-house next door nobody watched the hearth, and the flames crept along the beams into the building where you work. It's full of goods and tools, and old folk live upstairs.
ev.j_any_fire.text.10: A dry summer turned the quarter into kindling, and one spark was enough. The fire is already raging in the building where you work, and next door they're leading children out of a burning yard.
ev.j_any_fire.text.11: In the night a shop caught fire in the very building where you work – from a lamp, or from someone's malice. Acrid smoke stings your eyes, and the neighbors upstairs are pounding on the walls, calling for help.
ev.j_any_fire.text.12: Half the quarter is already ablaze: the fire moves from house to house faster than people can carry out their things. It has reached the building where you work. Black smoke and weeping hang over the street.
ev.j_any_fire.text.13: Someone left embers unquenched, and by midnight they'd grown into a real fire. The building where you work is crackling and smoking, and frightened children are crying in the yard next door.
ev.j_any_fire.text.14: The fire leaps from roof to roof as if alive. You ran to your workplace just as its roof caught too. Nearby an old woman is screaming that there are little ones still in the house next door.
ev.j_any_fire.text.15: On a windy night a stray spark set a thatched roof alight, and the wind drove the fire down the whole row. The building where you work is already burning, and the neighbors are running to you for help.
ev.j_any_fire.text.16: The cry of 'Fire!' woke the whole street. The building where you work is burning, and the flames are about to reach the goods. Neighbors are carrying little ones and old folk out of the next doors, and there aren't enough hands.
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.1: An old pain in your lower back has kept you awake for months. The physician takes out a vial of a thick, dark potion: 'Five drops at night. No more – it's treacherous.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.1.E03: An old pain in your lower back has kept you awake for months. The physician takes out a vial of thick, dark poppy juice: 'Five drops in wine at night. No more – it's treacherous.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.1.ISL: An old pain in your lower back has kept you awake for months. The physician takes out a vial of dark poppy juice: "Five drops in sherbet at night. No more – it is treacherous."
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.1.egypt: Your back has kept you awake for months. The healer takes out a vial of dark poppy juice – Theban, the most prized of all: 'Five drops in wine at night. No more – it's treacherous.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.2: Your back hurts so much you can't straighten up in the mornings. The herb woman from the next street brings a dark vial: 'Five drops at night and you'll sleep like a baby. But no more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.3: A traveling remedy-seller, hearing you groan as you got up from the bench, produced a small vial: 'For any pain. Five drops at night. It's dear – but your back will forget it ever hurt.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.4: A neighbor whose back also hurts swears that only the dark drops save him. He took you to his healer, who now hands you a vial: 'Five drops, and not one more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.5: Ever since you fell from a ladder your back aches day and night. The physician shakes his head: nothing is broken, but the pain will stay a long time. He sets a vial of thick potion on the table: 'Five drops at night. No more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.6: Night after night you toss and turn, your lower back burning as if pressed with coals. In the morning the physician came, kneaded your back, shook his head and took out a vial: 'This will ease the pain and give you sleep. Five drops – and don't even think of more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.7: Years of hard work have come back to haunt your back: you can neither sit nor lie down. The physician holds out a dark, bitter potion: 'Five drops at night. It's strong and treacherous – respect it.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.8: Back pain has become your constant companion. The physician says there is a remedy: the juice of a certain flower that brings sleep and makes you forget pain. 'Five drops. Any more and it's no longer medicine.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.9: The damp has got into your bones, and your back answers every change of weather. The physician, feeling your lower back, sighs and takes out a vial: 'Five drops before bed. And keep it well away from you during the day.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.10: You can't remember the last time you slept without back pain. The physician, after some hesitation, takes a vial of dark drops from his chest: 'It helps many. It ruins some. Five drops – no more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.11: The healer at the shrine, after hearing about your bad back, drew a vial from the folds of his robe: 'Prayer is prayer, but this is for the night. Five drops. Take no more – it's treacherous.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.12: After a long illness your back aches so that every movement is torment. The physician sets a little vial by your bed: 'Five drops at night and the pain will retreat. But remember: it's treacherous.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.13: They say the rich escape any pain with costly dark drops. Now the physician offers them to you – for the back that won't let you live: 'Five drops at night. No more, do you hear?'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.14: You've tried everything: poultices, herbs, charms. Your back won't let go. So the physician produces his last resort – a vial of thick, dark potion: 'Five drops. Not a drop more.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.15: An old back injury has woken up and won't let you work or sleep. The physician who has known you for years says plainly: 'There are drops. Five at night and you'll feel better. But they're like a friendly dog that will bite one day.'
ev.v_poppy_pain.text.16: An acquaintance, seeing you clutch your lower back, brought you a vial from his own physician: 'It helps me. Five drops at night and you sleep till morning. Just don't get carried away.'
ev.c_h_stomach.text.1: Maybe the market fish was yesterday's, maybe the well water has gone bad – but your stomach is so wrung out that for three days you haven't strayed far from home.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.2: At the festival you ate too much – and, it seems, something that wasn't fresh. For three days your stomach has been churning; you're pale and can't look at food.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.3: You couldn't resist and gorged on unripe fruit straight from the tree. The reckoning came by nightfall and still hasn't left.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.4: In the heat you drank from a stagnant pond because the well was too far. Now your stomach cramps, and you're running out back more often than you'd like.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.5: The mushrooms the neighbors brought looked lovely. They tasted lovely too. The night afterwards, not so much: your stomach is in knots, and you haven't got out of bed for two days.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.6: From your long journey you brought home not only news but a sickness: your stomach hurts, you've no appetite and no strength even to reach the door.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.7: The stew had sat in the heat for two days, but you finished it anyway – a shame to throw it out. What you came to regret was something else: for three days you haven't strayed from home.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.8: A stomach sickness is going around the street – half the neighbors have it. Now it's got you too: weakness, cramps, and not a crumb will go down.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.9: You grabbed a bite of something fried and very tasty from a street vendor. You never found out what it was, but your stomach won't forget it: for two days now you've been queasy and cramping.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.10: You were invited to a wealthy house and fed so lavishly that refusing would have been rude. You ate out of politeness, and now that politeness has kept you flat on your back for three days.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.11: After the downpour the well water went cloudy, but you have to drink something. A day later the cramps began, and half the street seems to be suffering the same.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.12: The fisherman swore the fish was this morning's catch. Evidently he meant some other morning. Your stomach hurts so much you can't straighten up.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.13: In the punishing heat food spoils in half a day, and you evidently didn't keep an eye on it. Your stomach has revolted: nausea, chills, and no strength even to sit up.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.14: You tried a spicy dish with some visiting merchants and praised it at length. Your stomach did not share your opinion: for three nights you haven't slept for the cramps.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.15: Whether from worry or bad food, your stomach has hurt for days now: eat and it hurts, don't eat and it hurts anyway. You've lost weight and look drawn.
ev.c_h_stomach.text.16: At the neighbors' wedding you celebrated for three days and ate everything in sight. Now for three days you've been paying for it: your stomach churns, and the mere smell of food makes you queasy.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.1: A wealthy traveler bought everything on your stall, even the things laid out just for show. He seemed to have no idea how to haggle – and you didn't teach him.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.2: Before the big festival the market was such a crush that your goods were gone by noon. You sat behind an empty stall counting the takings, unable to believe your eyes.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.3: The steward of a wealthy household ordered a whole batch from you for a grand wedding. He paid at once, and extra for the rush. You worked nights, but it was worth it.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.4: The trader at the next stall fell ill, and for a week all his customers came to you. You wished him a speedy recovery – almost sincerely.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.5: A band of pilgrims passing through town bought everything of yours they could carry on the road. They haggled badly and blessed generously.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.6: A grand lady stopped at your stall, said nothing for a long while, then pointed at the most expensive thing and didn't ask the price. You named one – with room to spare. She didn't even blink.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.7: A rumor that everything was about to get more expensive spread through town in a single morning. By evening your shelves were empty and your purse the opposite. Whether prices actually rose, nobody ever found out.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.8: You put out a piece you considered a failure – and some eccentric bought exactly that one at triple the price, praising 'the master's bold hand' at length. You didn't argue.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.9: A troop of soldiers camped outside town and needed everything at once. You sold off your stock in two days and for the first time in a year breathed easy.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.10: A merchant from distant parts, staying just one night, saw your work and bought everything you had: 'Nobody makes this where I'm from.' He left in the morning, and you kept smiling for a long time.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.11: You went out to trade in pouring rain when everyone else stayed home. There weren't many customers, but every one of them was yours. You came home that evening with a heavy purse and a soaked back.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.12: The elder praised your work in front of everyone, and the next morning there was a line at your stall. People praised, handled and bought – down to the last item.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.13: The shrine needed new things for a great festival, and its keepers chose you. They paid without haggling, as if heaven itself were bargaining on your behalf.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.14: You took a chance and bought in extra stock when everyone else was scared. You guessed right: a month later demand soared and the goods sold for triple. The neighbors still ask how you knew.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.15: A young rich man, out at the market on his own for the first time, decided haggling was beneath his dignity. He bought half your stall and left happy. So did you.
ev.a_lucky_sale.text.16: Before the wedding season everyone rushed to buy gifts, and your goods suddenly became the most wanted in the district. You couldn't wrap things fast enough and by evening were hoarse from talking.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.1: You've learned that {npc} secretly sold the family house – without asking you, passing {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} off as the sole heir. The money, they say, is already spent.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.1.E03: You've learned that {npc} secretly sold the family house – without asking you, on a forged deed. The money, they say, is already spent.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.2: A stranger came to you and politely asked you to collect your last belongings from the family house – it belongs to him now. {npc} sold it to him, claiming to be the sole heir. The money, they say, is already gone.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.3: At the market someone told you, sympathetically, that the family house now belongs to someone else: {npc} secretly sold it to a visiting merchant. You, a lawful heir, weren't even mentioned in the sale.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.4: You learned that {npc}, tangled up in debts, sold the house you grew up in – quietly, quickly and without asking you. The debts are paid, and your share vanished along with them.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.5: {npc} suddenly moved to another town and started living in style. It soon became clear what was paying for it: the family house had been sold, and no one had thought to tell you.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.6: An old neighbor, running into you, asked in confusion why you hadn't come when the house was sold. That's how you found out: {npc} had sold the family house, passing {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} off as the sole heir.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.7: You meant to spend a couple of days in the house where you grew up, but strangers opened the door. It turned out {npc} had sold the house back in spring without so much as a word. Your share along with it.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.8: {npc} came to you, avoiding your eyes, and confessed everything: the house you grew up in was sold in secret, at half its worth, and the money has long since been spent. Your share is gone.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.9: Returning from a long absence, you learned that the house where you grew up is no longer yours. {npc} sold it without you, telling the buyer there were no other heirs.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.10: The elder took you aside and quietly told you: the family house has been sold, and {npc} sold it alone – as if you didn't exist. The money is already spent.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.11: You learned that {npc} hastily sold the house you grew up in – for next to nothing, just to be quick about it. You weren't asked or called, and nobody seems to have any intention of giving you your share.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.12: As always, you were getting ready for the festival at the house where you grew up – and learned there was nowhere to gather anymore: {npc} had secretly sold it. The money, they say, is already spent.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.13: Passing the house where you grew up, you saw strangers rebuilding it. The new owner was surprised at your outrage: the house was bought fair and square, and the seller was {npc} – the sole heir, or so {g=npc_sex:he|she} said.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.14: The rumor turned out to be true: {npc} made a deal with a rich neighbor and sold him the family house, garden and all. The deal said not a word about you, and the money has already gone who knows where.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.15: You were the last to know: the whole district has long known that {npc} sold the house where you grew up and passed {g=npc_sex:himself|herself} off as the sole heir. People sympathize, but the money is already gone.
ev.d_sib_betrayal.text.16: {npc} didn't even try to deny it: yes, {g=npc_sex:he|she} sold the family house; yes, without you. 'You didn't need it anyway,' {g=npc_sex:he|she} snapped. The money is already spent.
